questions.stem: Which pair of consonants differs only in voicing?
questions.explanation: /f/ and /v/ are both labiodental fricatives; the only difference is that /v/ vibrates the vocal cords and /f/ does not. A voicing pair shares place and manner. /p/ and /s/, /m/ and /k/, /ŋ/ and /θ/ differ in more than voicing.

distractorRationale.a: /p/ is a plosive and /s/ is a fricative; they also differ in place
distractorRationale.c: /m/ is a nasal and /k/ is a plosive; they are not a pair
distractorRationale.d: /ŋ/ is a nasal and /θ/ is a fricative

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: From the words lettered A to D, choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters underlined: **th**in
questions.explanation: Thin begins with voiceless /θ/. Think shares that sound. Then, this and the verb breathe all have voiced /ð/. The letters th are doing two different jobs, and the paper tests whether you can hear the difference.

distractorRationale.d: Breathe (the verb) ends in voiced /ð/; breath the noun would have been /θ/

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: From the words lettered A to D, choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters underlined: mea**s**ure
questions.explanation: The s in measure is /ʒ/, the voiced palato-alveolar fricative. Vision has the same sound. Pressure and sure have voiceless /ʃ/; church has the affricate /tʃ/. Same letter s, different sounds.

distractorRationale.a: Pressure has /ʃ/, the voiceless partner of /ʒ/
distractorRationale.d: Church has /tʃ/, an affricate, not a fricative

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: The sound /ŋ/ in sing is best classified as a
questions.explanation: /ŋ/ is the velar nasal: air passes through the nose, and the vocal cords vibrate. It is the sound at the end of sing, tongue and bank. It is not a plosive, so there is no /g/ at the end of sing in RP.

distractorRationale.a: Plosives stop the air completely; /ŋ/ does not, and it is voiced
distractorRationale.c: Fricatives squeeze the air; /ŋ/ is a nasal, and it is voiced
distractorRationale.d: The voiced affricate is /dʒ/, as in judge

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: From the words lettered A to D, choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters underlined: **ch**urch
questions.explanation: Church begins and ends with the affricate /tʃ/. Watch ends with the same sound. Chef and machine have /ʃ/, because ch and ch-like spellings are not reliable. Ship is /ʃ/ from the start.

distractorRationale.a: Chef has /ʃ/, a French-origin spelling of sh
distractorRationale.b: Machine has /ʃ/, as in the vowel lesson's /iː/ example — the ch is not /tʃ/
distractorRationale.d: Ship has /ʃ/, the fricative, not the affricate

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: In which word is the letter b silent?
questions.explanation: Debt is pronounced /det/; the b is not sounded. The same silent b appears in doubt, climb and plumber. In about, number and able the b is a full /b/.

distractorRationale.c: Number sounds the b; plumber, by contrast, does not

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: Which word contains the initial consonant cluster /str/?
questions.explanation: Street begins with three consonants in a row: /s/ + /t/ + /r/. That is a cluster. Sit and set have a single initial /s/; sheet has /ʃ/, which is one sound, not a cluster of s plus h. Simplifying street to /sit/ or /srit/ is a pronunciation error.

distractorRationale.b: Sit has a single initial /s/, not a cluster
distractorRationale.c: Set likewise has only /s/ at the start
distractorRationale.d: /ʃ/ in sheet is one phoneme; sh is not /s/ plus /h/

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: Which word begins with the same consonant sound as know?
questions.explanation: The k in know is silent, so the word begins with /n/. Knee is the same: silent k, sounded /n/. Keen, king and school all begin with a sounded /k/. Matching the letter k is the trap; matching the sound /n/ is the task.

distractorRationale.d: School begins with /sk/, which includes a sounded /k/
